title: General Characteristics
orientation: This short chapter opens Book Three ('From the Renaissance to Hume') and functions as Russell's overview of what makes the 'modern' period distinct from the medieval one. He identifies two master trends -- the diminishing authority of the Church and the rising authority of science -- and traces how they reshape politics, culture, and the temper of philosophy itself, ending with a diagnosis of the persistent problem of social order that will occupy the rest of the book.
historical_background: Russell sketches, in broad strokes, the long political transition from monarchy to democracy (accelerated by the American and French Revolutions) and, in 1917, to socialism; the decline of the feudal aristocracy north of the Alps and its replacement by an alliance of kings and rich merchants; and the fifteenth-century moral and political anarchy of Italy that provoked Machiavelli's doctrines. He also places the Copernican theory (published 1543) and its later confirmation by Kepler and Galileo in the seventeenth century as the decisive scientific turning point of the era.
philosophical_problems: What replaces ecclesiastical authority once it declines, and what kind of authority does science actually exercise in its place?
Why does modern philosophy tend toward individualism and subjectivism, and where does this tendency lead if pursued to its extreme?
What is the relationship between scientific technique, the impulse to power, and the loss of concern for ends rather than mere process?
How can a durable and satisfactory social order be achieved, given that neither the ancient (Roman) nor the medieval (Church) solution to anarchy was adequate?

philosophers_discussed.name: Descartes
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Cited as the modern philosopher in whom the individualistic and subjective character of modern philosophy is 'very marked,' since he builds all knowledge from the certainty of his own existence and treats clearness and distinctness (both subjective) as criteria of truth.

philosophers_discussed.name: Spinoza
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Noted as an exception where the subjective/individualist tendency is 'not prominent.'

philosophers_discussed.name: Leibniz
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Cited as an instance of the subjective tendency reappearing in his doctrine of 'windowless monads.'

philosophers_discussed.name: Locke
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Described as objective by temperament but 'forced reluctantly' into the subjective doctrine that knowledge is of the agreement or disagreement of ideas, a view he found so repulsive that he escaped it only through inconsistency.

philosophers_discussed.name: Berkeley
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Cited as saved from complete subjectivism, after abolishing matter, only by an appeal to God that most subsequent philosophers regarded as illegitimate.

philosophers_discussed.name: Hume
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Cited as the culmination of empiricist subjectivism in a scepticism 'which none could refute and none could accept.'

philosophers_discussed.name: Kant
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Grouped with Fichte as subjective 'in temperament as well as in doctrine.'

philosophers_discussed.name: Fichte
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Cited, with Hegel, as an example of a German philosophical outlook 'totally unconnected with commerce,' and as subjective in temperament and doctrine.

philosophers_discussed.name: Hegel
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Noted as an exception to the commerce-linked 'liberal' culture of the age, and as 'saved' from pure subjectivism by the influence of Spinoza.

philosophers_discussed.name: Rousseau
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Credited, with the romantic movement, for extending subjectivity from theory of knowledge into ethics and politics, a line Russell traces forward to the complete anarchism of Bakunin.

philosophers_discussed.name: Bakunin
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Named as the logical endpoint of Rousseauian/romantic subjectivism extended into politics: 'complete anarchism.'

philosophers_discussed.name: Machiavelli
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Referenced as the thinker whose doctrines arose from the moral and political anarchy of fifteenth-century Italy, previewing Chapter III.

philosophers_discussed.name: Saint Augustine
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Invoked at the chapter's close: Russell argues the durable solution to social order requires combining 'the solidity of the Roman Empire with the idealism of Saint Augustine's City of God.'

schools_discussed: Scholastic philosophy (as the discipline modern philosophy reacted against)
Continental idealism / rationalism (in embryo, via Descartes, Leibniz, Spinoza)
British empiricism (in embryo, via Locke, Berkeley, Hume)

core_concepts.name: The shift from ecclesiastical to scientific authority
core_concepts.plain_explanation: The modern age is defined less by any single doctrine than by two linked changes: the Church stops being the ultimate authority over what people should believe and how society should be governed, and science gradually takes over as the authority people trust about the natural world.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell's framing thesis: 'the diminishing authority of the Church, and the increasing authority of science' are the two most important respects in which the modern mental outlook differs from the medieval, with the rejection of ecclesiastical authority (negative) preceding, historically, the acceptance of scientific authority (positive).
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It organizes the entire structure of Book Three: first the anarchic, pre-scientific Renaissance rebellion against the Church (Chapters II-V), then the rise of science and its philosophical consequences (Chapters VI onward).
core_concepts.historical_origin: Begins with the Italian Renaissance's turn to antiquity rather than science, and becomes decisive only with the Copernican theory (1543) as developed by Kepler and Galileo in the seventeenth century.
examples: The Italian Renaissance's opposition to the Church looked to a 'more distant past' (antiquity) rather than to science.
The Copernican theory of 1543, not influential until taken up by Kepler and Galileo
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Sets up the entire subsequent narrative of Book Three, from Machiavelli and the Reformation through the rise of science to Descartes and his successors.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly tied to the decline of the Church's governmental authority and its replacement by the national State.

core_concepts.name: The distinctive character of scientific authority
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Unlike the Church, which demanded belief on pain of punishment and claimed a complete, eternally fixed system covering all of morality and history, science persuades only by appeal to reason, covers only a small 'island' of what has been ascertained, and holds its conclusions tentatively, as probable rather than certain.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell's contrast: ecclesiastical authority is governmental, total, and dogmatically certain; scientific authority is 'piecemeal and partial,' intellectual rather than coercive, and 'made tentatively, on a basis of probability,' producing 'a temper of mind very different from that of the medieval dogmatist.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: This distinction explains why science, despite lacking coercive power, nonetheless displaced the Church as the dominant intellectual authority of the modern age.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Emerges alongside the rise of experimental and mathematical science in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.
examples: Science pronounces only on 'whatever, at the time, appears to have been scientifically ascertained'
competing_positions: Catholic dogma's claim to lay down 'a complete system, covering human morality, human hopes, and the past and future history of the universe'
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly contrasted with ecclesiastical governmental authority.

core_concepts.name: Subjectivism as the recurring character of modern philosophy
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Since Descartes, most modern philosophers have started from the certainty of their own mind or experience rather than from the external world, and this same individualistic, inward-looking tendency spread from theories of knowledge into ethics and politics, eventually reaching the extreme of philosophical anarchism.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell's diagnosis that 'modern philosophy... has retained, for the most part, an individualistic and subjective character,' traceable from Descartes's cogito through the British empiricists' difficulties with matter to Kant, Fichte, and finally Rousseau's extension of subjectivity to ethics and politics, 'ended, logically, in complete anarchism such as that of Bakunin.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell treats this trajectory as one of two 'forms of madness' afflicting modern thought, and frames the whole of Book Three partly as a history of this tendency and its consequences.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Begins with Descartes building 'all knowledge from the certainty of his own existence.'
examples: Locke's reluctant admission that knowledge is of the agreement or disagreement of ideas
Berkeley's abolition of matter, saved from subjectivism only by God
Hume's scepticism, 'which none could refute and none could accept'
Rousseau and Romanticism extending subjectivism to ethics and politics
competing_positions: Locke's and Hegel's partial resistance to pure subjectivism (Locke by temperament, Hegel via Spinoza's influence)
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Traced by Russell all the way to Bakunin's anarchism, which he calls 'a form of madness.'
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Extends, via Rousseau, directly into political theory and the critique of authority.

core_concepts.name: Science as technique and the 'power philosophy'
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Beyond science as a body of theory, there is 'practical science' -- technology -- which gives human beings, collectively rather than individually, immense power over nature. Because this power is ethically neutral (it says what can be done, not what should be done), and because it requires large-scale organization, it tends to produce philosophies obsessed with skillful process and control rather than with worthwhile ends.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell's account of practical science ('an attempt to change the world') as socially rather than individually empowering, requiring 'the co-operation of a large number of individuals organized under a single direction,' and as ethically neutral, giving rise to 'power philosophies' that 'tend to regard everything non-human as mere raw material' and value only 'the skilfulness of the process,' not ends -- which Russell calls 'the most dangerous form' of madness in his own day.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: This is Russell's second diagnosed 'form of madness,' complementing the anarchistic extreme of subjectivism, and he explicitly states that 'a sane philosophy should provide an antidote' to it -- framing the normative stakes of the entire book.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Traced to the practical use of science in warfare from Galileo and Leonardo onward, later extended to machine production and the use of steam and electricity.
examples: Galileo and Leonardo obtaining government employment through claims to improve artillery and fortification
The growth of machine production and the use of steam, then electricity
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Implicitly frames Russell's critical stance toward twentieth-century totalitarian 'power philosophies,' discussed later in the book.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly political: control of the 'vast organizations' that scientific technique requires determines what purposes power is put to.

core_concepts.name: The unresolved problem of social order: Rome versus the City of God
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Ancient civilization ended its chaos through the Roman Empire -- an actual, workable state, but merely a brute fact with no ennobling idea behind it. Medieval civilization proposed the Church as an ideal of universal order, but this idea was never fully realized in practice. Russell argues the modern world is drifting back toward a Rome-like solution (order imposed by force) and that a truly durable order needs both the practical solidity of Rome and the moral idealism of Augustine's City of God.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell's closing diagnosis: 'The ancient world found an end to anarchy in the Roman Empire, but the Roman Empire was a brute fact, not an idea. The Catholic world sought an end to anarchy in the Church, which was an idea, but was never adequately embodied in fact... The problem of a durable and satisfactory social order can only be solved by combining the solidity of the Roman Empire with the idealism of Saint Augustine's City of God.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: This is the chapter's final thesis and effectively states the normative problem that Russell implies the rest of modern philosophy -- and his own book -- must try to address.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Draws on Russell's earlier treatment of the Roman Empire (Book One) and of Augustine's City of God (Book Two).
competing_positions: A social order 'imposed by force, representing the will of the powerful rather than the hopes of common men' -- the direction Russell says the modern world seemed, in 1945, to be moving toward
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Frames the entire remainder of the History as, implicitly, a search for the 'new philosophy' Russell says will be needed.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Explicitly political and religious: contrasts the Roman state with the Christian ideal of the City of God.

arguments.title: From subjectivism in epistemology to anarchism in politics
premises: Modern philosophy, beginning with Descartes, has tended to ground knowledge in the certainty of the individual subject's own thought rather than in the external world.
This subjective, individualistic orientation, though checked in some thinkers (Locke, Hegel), persisted and even deepened through Kant and Fichte.
Rousseau and the romantic movement extended this same subjectivity out of epistemology into ethics and politics.
arguments.conclusion: This extension of subjectivism into politics 'ended, logically, in complete anarchism such as that of Bakunin,' which Russell calls 'a form of madness.'
arguments.explanation: Russell is not presenting a rigorous logical deduction but a historical-intellectual trajectory: he treats the philosophical starting point (the primacy of the subjective 'I') as carrying, when pursued to its extreme in ethics and politics, an anti-authoritarian, ultimately anarchistic charge.
implications: Frames one of Russell's two 'forms of madness' that a sound modern philosophy must guard against.
Implicitly critiques the entire epistemological tradition running from Descartes to the Romantics for its practical political consequences.

key_distinctions: Ecclesiastical (governmental, dogmatic, total) authority vs. scientific (intellectual, tentative, piecemeal) authority
Theoretical science (understanding the world) vs. practical science / technique (changing the world)
Individual power (as in earlier, pre-technological ages) vs. social power conferred by scientific technique
The Roman Empire as a 'brute fact, not an idea' vs. the Church as 'an idea... never adequately embodied in fact'
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Russell reaches back to Saint Augustine's City of God (treated in Book Two) as half of his proposed synthesis for a durable social order, and to the Roman Empire (Book One) as the other half, framing Book Three as continuous with these earlier historical themes.
connections_to_later_philosophers: This chapter previews virtually the entire cast of Book Three: Machiavelli (Ch. III), the Reformation figures (Ch. V), the founders of science (Ch. VI), and above all Descartes and his successors (Leibniz, Locke, Berkeley, Hume, Kant, Fichte, Hegel), whose shared subjectivist tendency is named here before being developed chapter by chapter later in the book.
political_social_context: Russell surveys the long-run political shift from monarchy toward democracy (accelerated by the American and French Revolutions) and then, in 1917, toward socialism; the decline of the feudal aristocracy and its replacement by an alliance of kings and rich merchants; and the specifically Italian crisis of political and moral anarchy that produced Machiavelli.
religion_science_culture_context: The chapter's central axis is religious-scientific: the decline of Church authority and the rise of scientific authority, including the delayed impact of the Copernican theory (1543) until Kepler and Galileo, and the subsequent 'long fight between science and dogma.'
russell_presentation: Russell frames the whole of Book Three around two intertwined historical movements: the decline of the Church's governmental and doctrinal authority, and the rise of science's very different, tentative, and piecemeal intellectual authority. He presents modern philosophy since Descartes as characteristically individualistic and subjective, tracing this thread through Leibniz, Locke, Berkeley, and Hume to Kant, Fichte, and finally Rousseau and the Romantics, whom he holds responsible for extending subjectivism into an anarchistic politics he calls 'a form of madness.' He balances this with a second, opposite danger: the 'power philosophies' generated by scientific technique, which treat everything non-human as raw material and value process over ends -- which he calls, more gravely, 'the most dangerous form' of madness of his own time, one 'against which a sane philosophy should provide an antidote.' He closes on a historical-political diagnosis rather than a purely philosophical one: neither the Roman Empire (an effective but merely factual order) nor the medieval Church (an ideal never fully realized) solved the problem of a durable social order, and he suggests -- without elaborating -- that a 'new philosophy' combining Rome's solidity with Augustine's idealism is still needed.
critical_context: Historical perspective: Russell was writing in 1943-44, during the Second World War, and his warning about 'power philosophies' that treat non-human (and by extension human) material instrumentally, and about a drift toward 'a social order imposed by force,' is widely read by commentators as a direct response to fascism and Soviet totalitarianism rather than a purely historical judgment about the Renaissance-to-Hume period; readers should note that this framing chapter carries more of Russell's own political anxieties of the 1940s than the more purely expository chapters that follow.
key_takeaways: The modern age, for Russell, is defined chiefly by the diminishing authority of the Church and the increasing (but very differently structured) authority of science.
Scientific authority is intellectual, tentative, and partial, in contrast to the Church's governmental, dogmatic, and total authority.

Practical science (technique) confers power that is social rather than individual, and tends, because it is ethically neutral, to generate 'power philosophies' focused on process rather than ends -- one of Russell's two 'forms of madness.'

Modern philosophy from Descartes onward has an individualistic, subjective character that Russell traces forward into Rousseau's romanticism and, at its extreme, into Bakunin's anarchism -- his other 'form of madness.'

Neither the ancient solution to anarchy (the Roman Empire, a fact without an idea) nor the medieval solution (the Church, an idea never fully realized) has adequately solved the problem of durable social order; Russell suggests a new philosophy combining both is needed.
study_notes:
Treat this chapter as a table of contents in disguise: almost every idea Russell raises here gets its own chapter later in Book Three. When you meet Machiavelli, the Reformation, Bacon, Hobbes, and especially Descartes and his successors, it is worth returning to this chapter's claims about subjectivism and 'power philosophy' and asking whether the later chapter actually bears them out. The two 'forms of madness' Russell names -- anarchistic subjectivism and power-obsessed technique -- are best understood as two failure modes of the same underlying shift: once external authority (the Church) no longer anchors belief or conduct, thought can spin inward toward the isolated self (subjectivism) or outward toward pure instrumental control (technique), and Russell suggests both extremes are dangerous.

The closing paragraph, contrasting the Roman Empire ('a brute fact, not an idea') with the Church ('an idea... never adequately embodied in fact'), is easy to skim past but is arguably the chapter's real thesis. Russell is not just describing history here; he is setting a normative problem -- how do you build a social order that is both effectively real and genuinely admirable? -- that implicitly motivates his own philosophical project and gives Book Three its underlying stakes, beyond the biographical and doctrinal detail of the chapters that follow.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The tendency in philosophy to treat one's own mind, experience, or point of view as the most certain starting point for knowledge, rather than the external world.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Russell's term for the individualistic epistemological orientation, originating with Descartes's cogito, in which certainty about one's own thought is prioritized over, and used as the basis for inferring, knowledge of the external world -- a tendency he traces through Leibniz, Locke, Berkeley, and Hume into Kant, Fichte, and Rousseau.
related_concepts: Subjectivism as the recurring character of modern philosophy

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A way of thinking, encouraged by science-as-technology, that cares only about whether something can be done efficiently, not about whether it should be done.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Russell's term for philosophies inspired by scientific technique that 'tend to regard everything non-human as mere raw material,' valuing 'the skilfulness of the process' over the goodness of ends, which he identifies as the most dangerous intellectual tendency of his own era.
related_concepts: Science as technique and the 'power philosophy'

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Theoretical science tries to understand the world; practical science (technology) tries to change it.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Russell's distinction between theoretical science, 'an attempt to understand the world,' and practical science, 'an attempt to change the world,' with the latter increasingly dominant from the sixteenth century onward and central to his account of the 'power philosophy.'
related_concepts: Science as technique and the 'power philosophy'

questions.prompt: According to Russell, what are the two most important respects in which the modern outlook differs from the medieval one?
questions.answer: The diminishing authority of the Church and the increasing authority of science.
questions.explanation: This is Russell's opening thesis for the whole of Book Three.

questions.prompt: How does Russell distinguish the authority of science from the authority of the Church?
questions.answer: The Church's authority is governmental and backed by penalties, and it claims a complete and eternally certain system covering morality, hopes, and history; science's authority is purely intellectual, appeals only to reason, is piecemeal (covering only what is currently ascertained), and is held tentatively as probable rather than absolutely certain.
questions.explanation: This contrast explains why science could displace ecclesiastical authority despite having no coercive power of its own.

questions.prompt: What historical trajectory does Russell trace from Descartes through Rousseau, and where does he say it 'logically' ends?
questions.answer: He traces a persistent individualistic, subjective character in modern philosophy from Descartes ('I think, therefore I am' as a foundation) through Leibniz, Locke, Berkeley, and Hume, to Kant and Fichte, and finally to Rousseau and the romantic movement, which extended subjectivity into ethics and politics, ending logically in the complete anarchism of Bakunin.
questions.explanation: Russell calls this extreme of subjectivism 'a form of madness.'

questions.prompt: Why does Russell say the power conferred by scientific technique is 'social, not individual'?
questions.answer: Because scientific technique requires the co-operation of a large number of individuals organized under a single direction; an average individual wrecked on a desert island could have achieved more in the seventeenth century than today, since modern power depends on collective organization, not personal skill alone.
questions.explanation: This grounds Russell's claim that scientific technique tends against anarchism and individualism, since it demands a well-knit social structure.

questions.prompt: Compare the two 'forms of madness' Russell identifies at the end of this chapter.
questions.answer: The first is the extreme of subjectivism extended into politics, culminating in anarchism such as Bakunin's. The second, which Russell calls the more dangerous of the two in his own time, is the 'power philosophy' generated by scientific technique, which treats everything non-human as mere raw material and values only the skillfulness of process, losing sight of ends.
questions.explanation: Both stem from the same root -- the erosion of an external, unifying authority (the Church) -- but push in opposite directions: one inward toward the isolated subject, the other outward toward pure technical control.

questions.prompt: What solution does Russell propose, at the chapter's end, for the problem of a durable and satisfactory social order?
questions.answer: He argues it can only be solved by combining the practical solidity of the Roman Empire with the moral idealism of Saint Augustine's City of God, since the ancient solution (Rome) was an effective fact without an ennobling idea, while the medieval solution (the Church) was an idea never adequately realized in fact.
questions.explanation: This is Russell's closing normative thesis, which frames the stakes of the rest of the book.

essay_prompts.prompt: Explain Russell's contrast between the authority of the Church and the authority of science in this chapter. Why, in his account, could science displace the Church's authority despite lacking any coercive power?

Explains the mechanism by which scientific authority persuades (appeal to reason alone)

essay_prompts.prompt: Russell identifies two 'forms of madness' in modern thought: subjectivism extended into anarchism, and 'power philosophy' generated by scientific technique. Evaluate whether these two tendencies are, as Russell implies, opposite responses to the same underlying historical cause (the decline of Church authority), or whether they are better understood as unrelated developments.
rubric: States both 'forms of madness' accurately with supporting textual evidence
Considers whether they share a common cause, as Russell implies
Engages with the critical_context point about the chapter's 1940s political context where relevant
